statement:
Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space with its Borel structure, \(\gamma=\operatorname{stdGaussian}(E)\) its centered standard identity-covariance Gaussian, and \(S=\{w\in E:\|w\|=1\}\). Let \(P\) be a probability law on \(E	imes\mathbb R\) with first marginal \(\gamma\), and let \(p\) be a real polynomial. Assume the response \((x,y)\mapsto y\) lies in \(L^2(P)\). For each probability \(\mu\) on \(S\), define the predictor, literal scalar potential and projected ambient gradient by the displayed formulas. Write \(g_\mu=
abla V_\mu\), and let \(\Pi(\mu,
u)\) denote all probability couplings. The potential integrand is integrable and the actual ambient gradient exists at every ambient weight. There are positive constants \(C_1,C_2\), chosen before all parameter laws and unit weights, for which \(G_\mu(w)\) is tangent, \(\|G_\mu(w)\|\le C_1\), \(Q(\mu,
u)<\infty\), and the displayed joint law/point estimate holds. The constants may depend on \(E,p,P\), including the response second moment. No independence of response and input, derivative witness, domination bound, mean bound, integral identity or gradient oracle is assumed. The cost is the explicit angular cost and the vector is the projected ambient gradient; no intrinsic path-length identity, installed manifold-gradient/Wasserstein API, generative model or full convergence theorem is asserted.
assumptions: \(E\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space with its Borel structure. Completeness is derived.
\(P\) is a probability measure on \(E\times\mathbb R\), and its first-coordinate pushforward is exactly \(\operatorname{stdGaussian}(E)\).
\(p\) is a finite real polynomial, and \((x,y)\mapsto y\) belongs to \(L^2(P)\). No independence is required.
\(S=\{w:\|w\|=1\}\). The display defines the literal predictor \(f_\mu\), potential \(V_\mu\), projection \(G_\mu\), and cost \(c(w,u)=\arccos\langle w,u\rangle\).
\(\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) is the set of all probability couplings. The extended nonnegative value \(Q(\mu,\nu)\) is proved finite before interpreting its real square root.
\(C_1,C_2>0\) are uniform over all subsequent probability laws and unit weights, but may depend on \(E,p,P\). No dimension-free or polynomial quantitative bound is asserted.

steps.title: Differentiate the Gaussian feature in L2
steps.text: Start with \(\Phi(w)(x)=p(\langle w,x\rangle)\) in \(H_0=L^2(\gamma)\). The existing Gaussian derivative theorem constructs its actual Fréchet derivative \(D_0(w)\), a uniform operator bound and an operator Lipschitz bound on the closed unit ball. No feature or derivative witness is an input.

steps.title: Pull the feature into the joint data space
steps.text: The input-marginal identity makes the first-coordinate projection measure preserving. Composition defines a linear isometry \(J:H_0\to H=L^2(P)\), even when response and input are dependent. Set \(F(w)=J\Phi(w)\) and \(D_P(w)=J\circ D_0(w)\). The isometry preserves both operator estimates.

steps.title: Identify the true parameter average
steps.text: Let \(\ell(x,y)=y\) in \(H\) and \(m_\mu=\int F(w)\,d\mu(w)\), a Bochner integral. The existing Gaussian averaging theorem puts the literal predictor in \(L^2(\gamma)\) and identifies its class with the feature mean. Pull back this identity and commute \(J\) with the Bochner integral. Thus \(m_\mu\) is the \(L^2(P)\) class of the predictor, and \(m_\mu-\ell\) represents the residual almost everywhere.

steps.title: Recover the literal scalar potential
steps.text: The residual and every ambient feature belong to \(L^2(P)\), so their product is integrable. The inner product and the almost-everywhere identities identify the literal potential with the displayed ambient function. This function identity is proved inside the theorem.

steps.title: Differentiate and identify the actual gradient
steps.text: Apply the existing quadratic feature-law theorem to \(F,D_P,\ell\) with the bounds just proved. Transport its ambient derivative across the function identity. Uniqueness identifies the displayed vector with the actual ambient gradient of the literal potential at every ambient weight.

steps.title: Project onto tangent directions
steps.text: For a unit weight, let \(P_wz=z-\langle z,w\rangle w\) and \(G_\mu(w)=P_w\nabla V_\mu(w)\). Substituting the gradient identity lets the feature-law theorem supply tangency and a positive uniform norm constant \(C_1\).

steps.title: Keep the angular cost and pass to joint law/point control
steps.text: Use \(c(w,u)=\arccos\langle w,u\rangle\) on \(S\), and take the infimum of \(\int c^2\,d\pi\) over all couplings. The feature-law parent proves finiteness of \(Q\) and the projected Hilbert-space estimate. Substitute the actual-gradient identity for both laws. The constants \(C_1,C_2\) precede every law and weight quantifier; they may depend on \(E,p,P\), including the response norm.

boundary: The theorem returns an actual ambient gradient and its explicit normal-component projection. Intrinsic path-length and installed Riemannian-gradient/Wasserstein API identifications are separate.
No teacher/noise generative construction, general stochastic model, convergence theorem or primary-textbook chapter completion is certified.
Derivative witnesses, domination, feature means, residual budgets and scalar-potential identities are constructed inside the proof. Constants remain qualitative and may depend on the dimension.
